source: Agrios Principles of Plant Infection Biology & Pathogenesis (Section 1)
text: Section 1: Spore Germination, Adhesion, and Surface Sensing Mechanics. Fungal plant pathogens initiate infection when reproductive propagules (conidia, ascospores, or motile oomycete zoospores) make physical contact with host aerial organs. Initial adhesion requires the secretion of mucilaginous extracellular matrices containing glycoproteins and hydrophobic cutin-binding proteins. Following adhesion, the pathogen senses specific physical topographical cues on the plant cuticle, such as stomatal guard cell lip ridges, vein depressions, or chemical stimuli like epicuticular wax long-chain fatty alcohols. For example, rust fungi (Uredinales) use precise thigmotropic (touch-sensitive) surface sensing to orient germ tube extension perpendicular to epidermal cells until encountering a stomatal aperture. Section 2: Appressorium Morphogenesis and Mechanical Penetration Mechanics. Upon locating an optimal penetration site, many phytopathogenic fungi (including Magnaporthe oryzae, Colletotrichum, and Venturia inaequalis) differentiate specialized domed infection cells termed appressoria. The appressorium develops a thick internal melanin pigment layer within its inner cell wall. This impermeable melanin matrix allows the accumulation of massive intracellular glycerol concentrations (exceeding 3 to 5 M), generating colossal hydrostatic turgor pressure up to 8.0 megapascals (MPa), equivalent to 80 times atmospheric pressure. At the center of the appressorial base, a rigid, needle-like penetration peg emerges, applying focused mechanical shearing force to physically rupture the hydrophobic plant cuticle.

Section 3: Enzymatic Degradation of the Host Cuticle and Cell Wall Complex. Simultaneously with mechanical pressure, phytopathogens secrete a battery of cell-wall-degrading enzymes (CWDEs) in a coordinated temporal sequence. First, cutinases and esterases hydrolyze insoluble cutin polymers into hydroxy fatty acids. Once the cuticle barrier is breached, the pathogen deploys pectin-degrading enzymes: pectin methyl esterases (PME) de-esterify homogalacturonan, followed by endopolygalacturonases (endo-PG) and pectate lyases (PL), which cleave alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds in the middle lamella. This causes maceration of plant intercellular cementing matrices. Subsequently, cellulolytic enzymes (endoglucanases, cellobiohydrolases, and beta-glucosidases) and hemicellulases (xylanases and xyloglucanases) break down the rigid cellulose microfibril network of primary and secondary plant cell walls. Section 4: Pathogen Trophic Lifestyles: Biotrophy, Necrotrophy, and Hemibiotrophy. Phytopathogens are classified by their nutritional acquisition strategy into three major lifestyles:
1. Obligate Biotrophs (e.g., powdery mildews such as Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe, downy mildews such as Pseudoperonospora cubensis, and rust fungi): These pathogens require living host cells to survive and complete their life cycle.

They do not kill host tissue upon entry; instead, they form specialized intracellular feeding invaginations called haustoria. The haustorium invaginates the host plasma membrane without rupturing it, creating an extra-haustorial matrix across which the fungus extracts host photosynthates, hexoses, and amino acids while suppressing host programmed cell death. 2. Necrotrophs (e.g., Botrytis cinerea grey mold, Alternaria solani early blight, Sclerotinia sclerotiorum): These pathogens rapidly kill host cells upfront through the secretion of non-host-specific phytotoxins (such as botrydial, alternariol, oxalic acid) and massive bursts of hydrolytic pectinases. They feed saprophytically on the dead, lysed cellular contents and necrotic debris. 3. Hemibiotrophs (e.g., Phytophthora infestans late blight, Venturia inaequalis apple scab, Fusarium oxysporum): These pathogens maintain an initial stealth biotrophic phase, colonizing host tissues without causing visible symptoms, before switching transitionally to an aggressive, destructive necrotrophic phase marked by extensive tissue water-soaking and necrosis. Section 5: Molecular Immunology: PTI vs. ETI and The Zig-Zag Zig Model. Plant innate immunity operates through a two-tiered receptor recognition system:
Tier 1: Pattern-Triggered Immunity (PTI). Cell surface pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as receptor-like kinases (RLKs) including FLS2 (recognizing bacterial flagellin peptide flg22), EFR (recognizing bacterial EF-Tu peptide elf18), and CERK1 (recognizing fungal chitin oligosaccharides), detect conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs / MAMPs).

text: PTI activation initiates calcium influx, an extracellular oxidative burst (superoxide and hydrogen peroxide), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation cascades, and deposition of callose polymer plugs at plasmodesmata. Tier 2: Effector-Triggered Susceptibility (ETS) and Effector-Triggered Immunity (ETI). Adapted pathogens deliver virulence effector proteins (via bacterial Type III secretion systems or oomycete RXLR/CRN translocation motifs) directly into host cells to suppress PTI signaling. In resistant plants, intracellular nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR / NBS-LRR) disease resistance (R) proteins directly or indirectly detect these specific pathogen effectors. Recognition triggers ETI: a prolonged, high-amplitude defense response that typically culminates in the Hypersensitive Response (HR)—localized, rapid programmed cell death that arrests pathogen spread.
